title: Guterres warns of 2.5°C warming as COP31 leaders meet; India presses for climate finance
dek: At the Antalya climate summit, the UN chief said current plans fall far short. India wants a formal work programme on climate finance and says adaptation goals must not be tied to access to money.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres told world leaders at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, that current national plans put the world on course for more than 2.5°C of warming, as India pressed developed countries to meet their legal obligation to provide climate finance.

"Our planet is heating up. The clock is winding down. It's make or bake time," Mr Guterres said on Wednesday at the opening of the two-day World Leaders' Summit, according to the UN's account of his speech. "We cannot demand that countries transform their economies while denying them the means to do so," he said, calling for what he described as a climate justice pact.

## What Guterres said

Mr Guterres said the nine largest oil companies had earned $95 billion in profits in a single quarter, while the fund set up to help vulnerable countries pay for loss and damage from climate disasters had received about $600 million. The Paris Agreement aims to hold warming well below 2°C and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels.

The conference, which opened on 9 November and runs until 20 November, brings together 197 countries and the European Union. Türkiye holds the presidency, while Australia's climate minister, Chris Bowen, serves as president of negotiations under a compromise reached last year. More than 100 heads of state and government were expected at the leaders' segment, according to reports. Prime Minister Narendra Modi was not expected to attend, according to reports before the summit that cited officials.

## India's position

In India's opening statement on Tuesday, delivered by Environment Secretary Narendra Bhooshan, India said public finance from developed countries "remained central to supporting climate action", according to reports. It asked for a formal decision launching a Climate Finance Work Programme to make developed countries' obligations under Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement more concrete. Article 9.1 says developed countries "shall provide financial resources" to help developing countries.

India wants that finance to be predictable and largely public and concessional, rather than in the form of loans and private investment. It also argued that indicators for the Global Goal on Adaptation should be voluntary and not be used as conditions for access to finance, and that the review of countries' mitigation efforts should remain "party-driven, facilitative and non-punitive". India's delegation is led by Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav. Earlier this month, Mr Yadav said India would not sign a COP31 pledge on electrification or back a roadmap to phase out fossil fuels.

## Why finance matters

The UN Environment Programme's Adaptation Gap Report 2026, released before the summit, estimated that developing countries need about $305 billion a year by 2035 to adapt to climate change, or about $420 billion adjusted for inflation, reports said. International public finance for adaptation was between $28.2 billion and $31.7 billion in 2024.

For India, which is among the countries most exposed to heat waves, floods and cyclones, the outcome on adaptation finance matters directly. In Bengal, the Sundarbans and the coastal districts face rising seas and stronger cyclones. Developed countries have argued in past negotiations that big emerging economies, including India and China, should contribute more, and that private finance must play a larger role.

## What happens next

Ministers arrive for the second week of talks, when draft texts on finance and adaptation are negotiated. The conference is scheduled to end on 20 November, though climate summits often overrun.
